title: Meet Anny Han: 2nd Place Winner of MDCC Vol.2!
content:
## _Meet Anny Han, a 3D fashion and graphic designer with a deep background in pattern making and garment construction.  
By bridging traditional techniques with digital tools, she created a realistic, emotionally resonant digital fashion, resulting to her award of 2nd Place in the _[_Marvelous Designer Creator's Contest Vol.2 " TOKYO CONTINUUM - 東京進化系 -"!_](https://connect.clo-set.com/contest/mdcc2025vol2)

* * *

![44e8b1862dea4ef4aeaac508b9fdf6ef](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202512/6db6acc9f1144f13a8bd11a6a0645519/images/44e8b1862dea4ef4aeaac508b9fdf6ef4.webp)[花と爆 (Hana to Baku)](https://connect.clo-set.com/detail/57c70236280a403997e3eef3deae4f99)

* * *

### **1\. Artist Introduction: please tell us about yourself.**

**Anny Han:** Hello, my name is Anny Han, and I am a 3D fashion and graphic designer.

I currently work in fashion product development, using CLO and Marvelous Designer to create realistic digital garments based on my background in pattern making and construction. I first started learning 3D to improve communication and speed within the development process, and it soon became an essential tool for expressing my own creative world.

I joined this contest to explore new styles and push myself beyond my usual workflow as a creator. Through this experience, I gained clearer direction in building my own aesthetic and artistic identity in 3D.

![5d97640ccfb84ee29598e03aeb2b69b9](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202512/6db6acc9f1144f13a8bd11a6a0645519/images/5d97640ccfb84ee29598e03aeb2b69b9image.png)

* * *

### **2\. We’d like to hear more about the art direction in your Creator’s contest 2025 Vol.3. What was the visual style you were aiming for?**

**Anny Han:** For this project, I aimed to express the **dual identity** experienced by many young people living in modern cities.

The “Bomb (ボム)” on the back and the “Flower (花)” in the hand symbolize the contrast between destruction and beauty, resistance and acceptance—visualizing the conflicting emotions that coexist within today’s youth.

The overall art direction focused on the **intersection of tradition and modernity**. Inspired by traditional Japanese silhouettes and textiles, I reinterpreted these heritage elements through a contemporary and functional lens. I incorporated delicate stitchwork inspired by **Sashiko** , a traditional Japanese embroidery technique, to bring a rhythmic and meditative craftsmanship to the garment.

To balance this with a modern sensibility, I added technical pockets and a bold graphic bag to enhance practicality, creating a bridge between the past and the future.

The flower motif, blooming like an explosion, serves as the centerpiece of the look—turning the garment into a powerful form of visual storytelling.

![3D 花と爆 \(Hana to Baku\) Model](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/marketplace/202505/57c70236280a403997e3eef3deae4f99/thumbnail/2.png?resize=1&f=webp&w=1680&fit=scale-down)

* * *

### **3\. Would you be able to give us a quick overview of the different tools you use in your pipeline with a focus on Marvelous Designer? Have you encountered any challenges and how have you overcome them?**

![a937a8de69ef46f0b15868e10901916c](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202512/6db6acc9f1144f13a8bd11a6a0645519/images/a937a8de69ef46f0b15868e10901916cimage.png)

**Anny Han:** I began by creating the garment 2D pattern in a CLO program. Thanks to my background in pattern making, building the base structure was not difficult, but I focused on ensuring the garment made structural sense in real life.

In Marvelous Designer, I refined the silhouette by adjusting ease, natural wrinkles, and three-dimensional shape. After assembling the garment, I conducted quick color tests directly inside MD to explore different palettes. Separating parts into UV areas allowed me to manage materials and colors more efficiently throughout the process.

* * *

### **4\. Are there any tips and tricks with Marvelous Designer that you can share with the community?**

**Anny Han:** One thing I’ve learned is that continuously studying other creators’ work is essential. Seeing different approaches and styles always pushes me to grow, and I still feel that I have a lot to learn.

Rather than relying only on my own habits, I try to broaden my perspective by observing how others use Marvelous Designer and how they express details.

These days, I believe combining Marvelous Designer with AI tools can elevate the quality of a project even further—whether for ideation, reference gathering, or enhancing the final presentation.

Staying open to new tools and new ways of working is, for me, the most important tip.

* * *

### Community Post Comments:
Comment 1: Beautiful design. I am new and seeing others work is so inspiring.🙂👍🏻
content_description: Showcasing Anny Han’s innovative fusion of traditional garment craftsmanship and cutting-edge 3D digital design to create emotionally compelling, award-winning fashion.

title: Raisin Cosplay’s Quest to Build the Perfect Skyrim Armor
content:
## _Ever wondered how to tackle complex props and armor using CLO? We sat down with_[ _Raisin Cosplay_](https://www.raisincosplay.com/) _to learn how she finally brought the iconic Skyrim Steel Plate Armor to life after years of trial and error. Read on to discover how she bridges the gap between digital patterns and physical EVA foam to create something truly spectacular._

* * *

![aa970d4cdbed4ca08e3fa833dce2d323](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202512/ecdb1e1b2b7d4cfa9f40619320321b4d/images/aa970d4cdbed4ca08e3fa833dce2d323Userspotlight_December.png)

**Hi Raisin Cosplay! We're incredibly excited to hear your story. Your journey started with a love for comics and sewing, eventually leading you to the world of cosplay. Could you tell us about that "aha!" moment when you realized you could combine these passions to create something truly special, like your incredible armor project?**

I started sewing at a very young age as a child and always read comics. That “aha!” moment for me came around 2012 when I discovered the word “cosplay” as I was researching comic conventions and Halloween costumes online. I found many videos and forum posts of cosplayers’ incredible costumes at San Diego Comic Con. I discovered that there were even groups dedicated to professional cosplays such as the 501st from Star Wars. I was amazed to see that the community was so rich and developed and even more amazed when I learned there was a comic con near me! I went to my first comic con the following summer in my first costume and that was that!

**You describe yourself as a "jack of many trades," mastering everything from EVA foam to 3D modeling. How has this versatile, hands-on approach influenced your work, and how does a powerful digital tool like CLO fit into your very physical creation workflow?**

I’ve always considered myself to be a patternmaker. I was very lucky to get into it early in life when my mother’s friend from the mosque who was a trained tailor offered to give me a couple sewing lessons. From there, getting into 3D modeling was a natural transition, especially for cosplay. I was in a robotics club in high school that gave me exposure to both 3D printing and 3D modeling early on. However, most of all, I think practice in patternmaking all these years trained my brain to be able to visualize the connection between 2D shapes and 3D shapes more easily. So with both those skills in hand, CLO just made sense. CLO allows me to experiment in the digital world much more than I was able to in the physical world by removing obstacles related to material cost and wastage.

  
![a5397c4a3d214ceb8c1d5b9fd5c4e15c](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202512/ecdb1e1b2b7d4cfa9f40619320321b4d/images/a5397c4a3d214ceb8c1d5b9fd5c4e15c63347-1644701466-1646825252.jpg)![e325a27392874a6ea25e1e8b75e89932](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202512/ecdb1e1b2b7d4cfa9f40619320321b4d/images/e325a27392874a6ea25e1e8b75e89932combined%20image.png)

**Let's talk about this stunning armor. What was the core inspiration? Was it based on an existing character or your own original concept? We'd love to hear the story behind it.**

The armor is a cosplay of an existing armor from the 2011 video game “The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim.” It is the Steel Plate Armor, originally designed by Ray Leder, Senior Concept Artist at Bethesda Game Studios. I have always loved this design and have wanted to bring it to life for many years. In fact, I have unsuccessfully tried to create this armor twice before over the years and was not able to make it happen until I started using CLO!

![42d6a10eb06b4fc5932436f88aefebb8](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202512/ecdb1e1b2b7d4cfa9f40619320321b4d/images/42d6a10eb06b4fc5932436f88aefebb8Screenshot%202025-11-25%20222032.png)

**When you were creating the patterns for this armor in CLO, what were the most critical details you had to get right to ensure they would translate perfectly into physical materials like EVA foam? Perhaps there was a specific curve, seam, or layered piece that was especially challenging?**

Something I had to consider when translating the pattern onto EVA foam and engraving it is the “turn of cloth” of the foam. I used 4-5mm EVA foam, which is much thicker than most fabrics or leathers. Due to the thickness of the foam, the outside surface area of the armor is larger than the inside. Usually when cutting EVA foam, I would translate and cut the pattern on the “wrong” side of the foam that would be my interior surface area. However, this was not possible for this project as I had to engrave and cut the patterns on the “right” or exterior facing side of the foam. In order for the armor to fit me after cutting and assembling, the actual pattern had to be a bit larger. CLO’s additional thickness rendering was very helpful in doing this! The new “Extrusion Direction” setting will be especially vital for future projects.

![ea46376316e7495693e9dc10d42a601e](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202512/ecdb1e1b2b7d4cfa9f40619320321b4d/images/ea46376316e7495693e9dc10d42a601evlcsnap-2025-07-06-23h56m06s112.png)![4b06830369bc4e80b47c88a45cd098a3](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202512/ecdb1e1b2b7d4cfa9f40619320321b4d/images/4b06830369bc4e80b47c88a45cd098a3vlcsnap-2025-07-06-22h55m41s475.png)

**This is the part our users will be most excited about! Could you walk us through the process of taking your finished CLO patterns and turning them into the physical, wearable costume? What were the biggest hurdles in translating the 3D design into tangible materials?**

In my previous attempts, the biggest hurdle with trying to make this costume a reality was drawing out all the swirly engravings and having them flow seamlessly and symmetrically from pattern piece to pattern piece. I could not have done that efficiently without CLO! CLO also allowed me to export everything as a vector PDF to be able to turn the pattern pieces into laser engraving files. I love having the ability to use and export the files that way so they can be used with many other different software programs.

The final armor is made of high density EVA foam (also known as craft foam). I cut and engraved all the patterns onto sheets of 4mm thick foam with a simple 10 watt diode laser engraver. Once the patterns were cut and engraved, it was a matter of gluing all the seams with contact cement and using heat to achieve the final shapes and curves. From there, I sealed and hand painted the armor using various craft paints to get that patinated metallic finish!

![485e3b629186462e969500b6dcaf639e](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202512/ecdb1e1b2b7d4cfa9f40619320321b4d/images/485e3b629186462e969500b6dcaf639esteel-animeNJ-2025-06.jpg)

**You work in fashion retail and have a master's degree in business, which is a unique combination for a cosplayer. How does your professional background influence your creative projects?**

My job mainly funds my creative projects, but I’ve always been passionate about clothing. My background advises the more business side of things, like how I choose what kinds of patterns to create and how to market not only my digital products, but myself as well. I think my career has given me a wide variety of skills to be able to turn my creativity into a business including giving me an eye for product and skills for understanding my customers.

**Finally, many CLO users dream of bringing their digital creations to life, just as you have. What is one key piece of advice you would give to someone who wants to start their journey from digital design to physical cosplay or creation?**

For me, it’s been really important to learn by starting with a project I’m really passionate about. I find it hard to motivate myself if the project isn’t interesting. If you have an idea you care deeply about, use it to push yourself to develop the skills to make your idea a reality.
content_description: This page shares Raisin Cosplay’s inspiring journey of using CLO’s digital pattern-making tools to successfully design and create the iconic Skyrim Steel Plate Armor from virtual concepts to detailed, wearable EVA foam cosplay.

title: Copy as 3D Line tool or 3D Line Conversion from 2D Pattern for the CLO3D
content:
Helloooo, this is April. I'm still pretty new and learning CLO3D, but I pretty much use it everyday as a fashion designer. I see that you have this Copy as 3D Line tool or the 3D Line Conversion from 2D Patterns in some other version of CLO, but not in the one I use, which confuses me. It would save me hours spent tracing the same lines from a 2D Pattern if I could use this tool. My idea was that I could alter these 2D Patterns to make even cooler shapes based on my preference or the design piece (so the added garment is a base piece that I would alter to fit my design), which is why I was looking forward to using this tool, but it unfortunately doesn't seem to exist in the most updated version of CLO i use. So, I was wondering if this tool can be brought into the version of CLO3D I use?

### Community Post Comments:
Comment 1: Oh another feedback is that I do a lot of creating from scratch using the 3D Pen Avatar tool. And it would be totally great if there's a function to just copy and paste those 3D Pen Avatar lines or offset it (like you could do in the 2D Window on 2D Patterns). Right now I'm tracing the same 3D Pen Avatar Line and doing another one on the side, but it's parallel, and having the copy and paste tool or an offset tool for the 3D Pen Avatar tool would save me a lot of time too.

Comment 2: Oh, I tried googling online about it, but I guess it just doesn't exist yet. I come from an architecture background where I'm more familiar with Rhino5 features, and figured there'd be a tool that can do the same. Let me think. So, I guess this is just user feedback that I feel like CLO3D could improve on. In CLO3D, there's the process where you can generate a 2D pattern after flattening it from the 3D Pen line, so that they could be cut after to make an actual garment piece. I wish there was a way to back track that where say you start with the 2D Pattern (like you import any CLO garment file), and then you can generate the 3D lines from that. Why I wanted it was so I can use those 3D lines as a base to alter it into a new design - something new but similar enough to that base design that I chose (that already exists). But, it seems that CLO3D doesn't have that function yet. So, I guess it's now more of a user feedback. Would be cool if you could update CLO3D with this feature. It would save me hours of work time for sure :)

Comment 3: Hi. We are not sure what tool you are talking about. Do you have images we can reference to see?
content_description: This page aims to gather feedback and explore the possibility of adding the 3D Line Conversion tool from 2D Patterns into the current version of CLO3D to improve workflow for fashion designers.

title: Could anyone help why my 3D view not visible properly
content:

Comment 2: Hi! Welcome to the software! It can be a little tricky at times, no worries, it’s all a process of learning the software. If the other comment suggestion didn’t work, I was going to suggest you use arrangement points again, get it situated where you want it, and resimulate. Here’s how to access the arrangement points, I included a photo of where to find this. Once the blue dots appear, have your pattern piece highlighted and click on the blue dot where you’d like the garment to go on the body. Hope this helps!

Comment 3: Your garments are sitting slightly inside of your avatar. Fastest fix will likely be to Select all Pattern pieces > use your Gizmo in 3D to then pull the pieces slightly forward so they are no longer inside the avatar and simulate again
